claim: Normative models can account for learning in dynamic environments but have not yet been applied to faster decision processes.
source: Normative models can account for learning in these environments but have not yet been applied to faster decision processes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a gap in the literature that the current work addresses.

claim: The normative formulation of adaptive learning models acts as a leaky accumulator with non-absorbing bounds.
source: We present a novel, normative formulation of adaptive learning models that forms decisions by acting as a leaky accumulator with non-absorbing bounds.
evidence: This is the main theoretical contribution described in the abstract.

claim: The dynamics of the normative model depend on the expected rate of change of the statistics of the evidence.
source: These dynamics, derived for both discrete and continuous cases, depend on the expected rate of change of the statistics of the evidence and balance signal identification and change detection.
evidence: This is stated as a key property of the model in the abstract.

claim: Human subjects learned expectations about the rate of change, albeit imperfectly.
source: We found that, for two different tasks, human subjects learned these expectations, albeit imperfectly, then used them to make decisions in accordance with the normative model.
evidence: This is a main empirical finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Human subjects used learned expectations to make decisions in accordance with the normative model.
source: We found that, for two different tasks, human subjects learned these expectations, albeit imperfectly, then used them to make decisions in accordance with the normative model.
evidence: This is a main empirical finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) and drift-diffusion model are forms of belief-updating rules based on perfect integration over time of the logarithm of the likelihood ratio.
source: The sequential probability ratio test (SPRT), drift-diffusion model, and related sequential-sampling models are forms of 'belief-updating' rules for this normative process, based on perfect integration over time of the logarithm of the likelihood ratio (LLR) associated with each data point (Barnard, 1946; Wald, 1947; Good, 1979; Link, 1992; Gold and Shadlen, 2001; Smith and Ratcliff, 2004; Bogacz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Standard sequential-sampling models are normative only when the ideal starting time-point for accumulation is known.
source: These models have been useful for studying neural mechanisms of decision-making (Gold and Shadlen, 2007) but are normative for only a restricted set of conditions in which: (1) the ideal starting time-point for accumulation is known (e.g., given by the onset of an experimental trial); and (2) the statistics of the incoming information are perfectly stable throughout the entire sequence, with no change in the underlying signal and all noise coming from the same probability distribution.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing models with citation support.

claim: Standard sequential-sampling models are normative only when the statistics of the incoming information are perfectly stable throughout the entire sequence.
source: These models have been useful for studying neural mechanisms of decision-making (Gold and Shadlen, 2007) but are normative for only a restricted set of conditions in which: (1) the ideal starting time-point for accumulation is known (e.g., given by the onset of an experimental trial); and (2) the statistics of the incoming information are perfectly stable throughout the entire sequence, with no change in the underlying signal and all noise coming from the same probability distribution.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing models with citation support.

claim: Perfect integration can be problematic for tasks that require the detection of signal changes.
source: Perfect integration can be particularly problematic for tasks that require the detection of signal changes (Clifford and Ibbotson, 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Integrating evidence at the wrong time might miss the signal or add unnecessary noise, resulting in a loss of sensitivity to the change.
source: However, when there is temporal uncertainty about the change, integrating evidence at the wrong time might miss the signal or add unnecessary noise, resulting in a loss of sensitivity to the change (Lasley and Cohn, 1981).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The normative model is based on Bayesian principles that have typically been used to understand learning processes in dynamic environments on relatively slow timescales.
source: We derived a belief-update rule for these kinds of decisions based on Bayesian principles that have typically been used to understand learning processes in dynamic environments on relatively slow timescales (Figure 1A) (Yu and Dayan, 2005; Adams and MacKay, 2007; Behrens et al., 2007; Fearnhead and Liu, 2007; Wilson et al., 2010; McGuire et al., 2014; Sato and Kording, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The belief-update rule relates directly to models of perfect, leaky, and bounded accumulation that have been used to understand decision processes in stable environments.
source: This rule both accounts for environmental instability and relates directly to models of perfect, leaky, and bounded accumulation that have been used to understand decision processes in stable environments (Link, 1992; Gold and Shadlen, 2001; Usher and McClelland, 2001; Smith and Ratcliff, 2004; Bogacz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Belief is defined as the logarithm of the posterior odds of the alternative sources of information given all information collected until a given time point.
source: We define belief as the logarithm of the posterior odds of the alternative sources of information (L) given all information collected until a given time point.
evidence: This is a definitional statement in the model description.

claim: The sign of L indicates which source is currently believed to be generating the information.
source: The sign of L indicates which source is currently believed to be generating the information, and the magnitude of L indicates how certain that belief is.
evidence: This is a definitional statement in the model description.

claim: The magnitude of L indicates how certain that belief is.
source: The sign of L indicates which source is currently believed to be generating the information, and the magnitude of L indicates how certain that belief is.
evidence: This is a definitional statement in the model description.

claim: The update rule is optimal when there is a fixed probability that the source could switch to the alternative at any time according to a Bernoulli process.
source: The update rule is optimal when there is a fixed probability that the source could switch to the alternative at any time (i.e., according to a Bernoulli process).
evidence: This is stated as a condition for optimality of the model.

claim: For H = 0 (perfect stability), the update equation reduces to perfect accumulation as in random-walk and related decision models.
source: For the special case of H = 0 (perfect stability), the two rightmost terms in Equation 2 cancel. In this case, the update Equation 1 reduces to perfect accumulation as in random-walk and related decision models used to identify steady, but noisy, signals (Figure 1D) (Smith and Ratcliff, 2004; Bogacz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 1D and citations.

claim: When H is high and changes are expected, accumulation over time is severely limited to facilitate change detection.
source: In contrast, when H is high and changes are expected, accumulation over time is severely limited to facilitate change detection (Figures 1F, 2G).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figures 1F and 2G.

claim: For H = 0.5, the history of evidence is irrelevant at all times and Ln = LLRn.
source: Finally, in the special case of H = 0.5, the history of evidence is irrelevant at all times and all three terms in Equation 2 cancel, so ψ = 0 and Ln = LLRn.
evidence: This is stated as a special case of the model.

claim: When beliefs are uncertain (regimes around Ln − 1 = 0), the model acts like a leaky accumulator.
source: First, when beliefs are uncertain (i.e., regimes around Ln − 1 = 0 in Figures 1B, 2A,C; Equation 3a, in which Kn predominates over θn), the model acts like a leaky accumulator, in which the prior expectation is a fraction of the previous belief (Busemeyer and Townsend, 1993; Usher and McClelland, 2001; Bogacz et al., 2006; Tsetsos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with reference to figures and citations.

claim: The normative leak is adaptive and directly dependent on H.
source: In this regime, the normative leak is adaptive, which has been demonstrated previously (Ossmy et al., 2013), and is directly dependent on H, which has not been described previously.
evidence: This is stated with citation for adaptive leak and claim of novelty for H-dependence.

claim: For low H and thus relative stability, a small leak provides long integration times.
source: For low H and thus relative stability, a small leak provides long integration times.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the model.

claim: For H ≈ 0.5, the model discards all historical information and L depends only on LLR.
source: For H ≈ 0.5 (the correct answer is equally likely to stay or switch after each sample), the model discards all historical information and L depends only on LLR.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the model.

claim: For H > 0.5, the prior expectation undergoes damped oscillations.
source: For H > 0.5 (the correct answer is more likely to switch after each sample), the prior expectation undergoes damped oscillations (Figure 2G), even when the source of evidence is transiently stable.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 2G.

claim: As the magnitude of Ln − 1 increases and belief certainty becomes high, the prior expectation approaches a 'stabilizing boundary' whose height directly depends on H.
source: Second, as the magnitude of Ln − 1 increases and belief certainty becomes high (i.e., regimes around Ln − 1 far from zero in Figures 1B, 2A,C; Equation 3b,c, in which θn predominates over Kn), such as when the incoming evidence is strong or during periods of stability in the source, the prior expectation approaches a 'stabilizing boundary' whose height directly depends on H.
evidence: This is stated with reference to figures and equations.

claim: The stabilizing boundary represents a suspension of the accumulation process but does not terminate the decision process.
source: This boundary represents a suspension of the accumulation process but, unlike the decision bound in the SPRT and related models (Barnard, 1946; Wald, 1947; Good, 1979; Link, 1992; Smith and Ratcliff, 2004; Bogacz et al., 2006; Gold and Shadlen, 2007), does not terminate the decision process.
evidence: This is stated with citations to contrast with other models.

claim: The stabilizing boundary stabilizes Ln when no changes occur while still allowing for the sampling of new evidence that might lead to changes in belief.
source: Instead, it stabilizes Ln when no changes occur (i.e., temporarily ending further evidence accumulation) while still allowing for the sampling of new evidence that might lead to changes in belief and a re-start of the accumulation process (Resulaj et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The stabilizing boundary is in contrast to the asymptote in leaky accumulation, which increases linearly with the strength of evidence.
source: The stabilizing boundary is also in contrast to the asymptote in leaky accumulation, which increases linearly with the strength of evidence (Busemeyer and Townsend, 1993; Usher and McClelland, 2001; Bogacz et al., 2006; Tsetsos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to contrast with other models.

claim: The trade-off between identification of steady signals and change detection depends on both evidence strength and expected H.
source: Together these properties navigate an inherent trade-off between identification of steady signals and change detection. This trade-off depends on both evidence strength and expected H (Figure 2E,G).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 2E,G.

claim: For weak evidence, the trade-off is most severe, as the model uses expected H to err on the side of either detecting changes quickly when H is high or identifying stable signals when H is low.
source: For weak evidence, the trade-off is most severe, as the model uses expected H to err on the side of either detecting changes quickly when H is high or identifying stable signals when H is low.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the model.

claim: As the strength of evidence increases, performance improves steadily for both conditions and the trade-off diminishes.
source: As the strength of evidence increases, performance improves steadily for both conditions and the trade-off diminishes.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the model.

claim: The continuous-time model is based on the optimal filter for a Markov jump process with two states and stationary white-noise emissions.
source: The model is based on the optimal filter for a Markov jump process with two states and stationary white-noise emissions (Zakai, 1965; Liptser and Shiryaev, 1977; Crisan and Rozovskii, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: In the special case that λ = 0, dL(t) = Adx(t), which is perfect integration of the noisy observations dx(t).
source: In the special case that λ = 0, dL(t) = Adx(t), which is perfect integration of the noisy observations dx(t).
evidence: This is stated as a special case of the continuous-time model.

claim: When beliefs are uncertain (L ≈ 0), dL ≈ −2λLdt + Adx(t), which results in an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process over periods in which the source is perfectly stable.
source: When beliefs are uncertain (L ≈ 0), dL ≈ −2λLdt + Adx(t), which results in an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process over periods in which the source is perfectly stable (Busemeyer and Townsend, 1993; Bogacz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Subjects adapted, albeit imperfectly, to different hazard rates in the triangles task.
source: For both tasks, we found that: (1) subjects adapted, albeit imperfectly, to different hazard rates (via comparisons to a suboptimal model, which ignored block-wise changes in H) and used their subjective estimates of hazard rate in a manner consistent with the normative model
evidence: This is stated as a main finding for both tasks.

claim: Subjects used their subjective estimates of hazard rate in a manner consistent with the normative model in the triangles task.
source: For both tasks, we found that: (1) subjects adapted, albeit imperfectly, to different hazard rates (via comparisons to a suboptimal model, which ignored block-wise changes in H) and used their subjective estimates of hazard rate in a manner consistent with the normative model
evidence: This is stated as a main finding for both tasks.

claim: Choice dynamics in the triangles task were better described by the normative model than by an accumulator with a leak that could vary as a free parameter for each hazard-specific block of trials but no stabilizing boundary.
source: and (2) their choice dynamics were better described by the normative model than two other adaptive, but suboptimal, alternatives inspired by the approximations to the normative model (one was an accumulator with a leak that could vary as a free parameter for each hazard-specific block of trials but no stabilizing boundary; the other was a perfect accumulator with a stabilizing boundary that could vary as a free parameter for each hazard-specific block of trials; see Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as a main finding with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Choice dynamics in the triangles task were better described by the normative model than by a perfect accumulator with a stabilizing boundary that could vary as a free parameter for each hazard-specific block of trials.
source: and (2) their choice dynamics were better described by the normative model than two other adaptive, but suboptimal, alternatives inspired by the approximations to the normative model (one was an accumulator with a leak that could vary as a free parameter for each hazard-specific block of trials but no stabilizing boundary; the other was a perfect accumulator with a stabilizing boundary that could vary as a free parameter for each hazard-specific block of trials; see Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as a main finding with reference to Figure 3.

claim: In the triangles task, subjects could make choices based on accumulated evidence after each new sample of data, with the LLR for each star corresponding to its position relative to each triangle.
source: This task required subjects to make trial-by-trial choices about which of two spatially separated triangles on a computer screen was the source of a single data point presented on that trial, represented as the position of a star on the screen (Figure 4A,B). Subjects could thus make choices based on accumulated evidence after each new sample of data, with the LLR for each star corresponding to its position relative to each triangle.
evidence: This is stated in the task description with reference to Figure 4A,B.

claim: In the triangles task, the correct source changed at a hazard rate that was constant within a block of trials but varied across blocks (0.05–0.95).
source: The correct source changed at a hazard rate that was constant within a block of trials but varied across blocks (0.05–0.95).
evidence: This is stated in the task description.

claim: In a subset of triangles task sessions (65 of 111), learning was facilitated by beginning and ending each block of trials with stretches of trial-by-trial feedback about the correct answer.
source: In a subset of sessions (65 of 111), learning was facilitated by beginning and ending each block of trials with stretches of trial-by-trial feedback about the correct answer.
evidence: This is stated in the task description.

claim: Subjects in the triangles task were never instructed on what the hazard rates were or when they would change.
source: However, subjects were never instructed on what the hazard rates were or when they would change.
evidence: This is stated in the task description.

claim: Models that allowed subjective H to freely vary by block provided better fits to the triangles task data than a suboptimal model that ignored the block-wise changes in objective H.
source: Specifically, models that allowed subjective H to freely vary by block provided better fits to the data than a suboptimal model that ignored the block-wise changes in objective H (median ± bootstrapped SEM difference of Bayesian Information Criterion, or BIC, from normative vs block-independent H fits was −23.721 ± 9.671, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.0001; per subject, the normative fits were better in 43 of 48 subjects using a signed-rank test, Bonferroni corrected p < 0.05).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: The normative model performed well on the triangles task, with choice residuals centered around zero (mean ± std deviance residual = 0.003 ± 0.458).
source: Overall, the normative model performed well, with choice residuals centered around zero (mean ± std deviance residual = 0.003 ± 0.458) and a reasonably close match to the choice data (median ± bootstrapped SEM McFadden's r2 of 0.895 ± 0.016 across subjects).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: The normative model had a reasonably close match to the triangles task choice data (median ± bootstrapped SEM McFadden's r2 of 0.895 ± 0.016 across subjects).
source: Overall, the normative model performed well, with choice residuals centered around zero (mean ± std deviance residual = 0.003 ± 0.458) and a reasonably close match to the choice data (median ± bootstrapped SEM McFadden's r2 of 0.895 ± 0.016 across subjects).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: The estimated values of subjective H from the triangles task fits were strongly correlated with objective H across all subjects (Pearson's r = 0.721, p < 0.0001).
source: Moreover, the estimated values of subjective H from these fits were strongly correlated with objective H across all subjects (Pearson's r = 0.721, p < 0.0001; Figure 4C)
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence and reference to Figure 4C.

claim: In the triangles task, 47 of 48 individual subjects showed a regression slope of subjective on objective H that was >0.
source: with 47 of 48 individual subjects showing a regression slope of subjective on objective H that was >0 and in 46 of those cases was also <1 (Figure 4D, median ± bootstrapped SEM regression slope = 0.402 ± 0.042).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence and reference to Figure 4D.

claim: In the triangles task, subjects' subjective estimates of H tended towards H ∼ 0.5.
source: However, although the subjects adapted their decision-making behavior appropriately for different values of H, their subjective estimates of H tended towards H ∼ 0.5, for which the history of evidence is irrelevant.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: The tendency to mis-estimate extreme hazard rates in the triangles task did not appear to reflect insufficient learning opportunities.
source: This tendency to mis-estimate extreme hazard rates did not appear to reflect insufficient learning opportunities, because these trends persisted even when restricting fits to the last 200 trials of each block (across subjects and blocks, bootstrapped regression slope of subjective on objective H = 0.373 ± 0.044; see also Figure 4—figure supplement 1) or to blocks beginning with explicit, trial-to-trial feedback (regression slope = 0.562 ± 0.038).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: When certainty was high in the triangles task, subjects consistently showed hazard-dependent biases that were predicted by the stabilizing boundary of the model.
source: When certainty was high (i.e., choices just following a trial in which the star position was far to the left or right), the subjects consistently showed hazard-dependent biases that were predicted by the stabilizing boundary of the model: weak evidence interpreted as stability for low H and change for high H (Spearman's r = 0.890, p < 0.0001, comparing predicted and actual biases from individual blocks; Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence and reference to Figure 5A,B.

claim: When weak evidence persisted without change-points for a run of trials following a change-point in the triangles task, choice dynamics consistently reflected the hazard-dependent leak predicted by the model.
source: When weak evidence persisted without change-points for a run of trials following a change-point, choice dynamics consistently reflected the hazard-dependent leak predicted by the model (Figure 2G, Figure 5D,E): gradual updates for low subjective H, immediate updates for subjective H ≈ 0.5, and damped oscillations for high subjective H (including lower accuracy on two vs one trial following the change-point).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 2G and Figure 5D,E.

claim: Fits to the block-independent model did not show H-dependent choice dynamics in the triangles task.
source: Fits to the block-independent model did not show these H-dependent choice dynamics, confirming that the choice dynamics did not result from any differences in how the randomly generated stars were sampled under the different conditions used for these analyses (Figure 5C,F).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 5C,F.

claim: In the triangles task, subjects' decision processes reflected a strong, hazard- and evidence-strength-dependent trade-off between detecting changes and identifying steady signals, as predicted by the normative model.
source: Second, the subjects' decision processes reflected a strong, hazard- and evidence-strength-dependent trade-off between detecting changes and identifying steady signals, as predicted by the normative model (Figure 5G–L).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 5G–L.

claim: In the triangles task with weak evidence, accuracy following a change-point was highest for high H (73.7 ± 2.4% correct) then declined steadily for intermediate (66.4 ± 1.2%) and low H (50.0 ± 7.3%).
source: When the evidence was weak (star positions close to the midline), accuracy following a change-point was highest for high H (mean ± bootstrapped SEM across blocks = 73.7 ± 2.4% correct) then declined steadily for intermediate (66.4 ± 1.2%) and low H (50.0 ± 7.3%; Spearman's correlation between change-point accuracy and H was 0.559, p < 0.0001, vs a predicted correlation from the normative model of 0.651).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: In the triangles task with weak evidence, accuracy on non change-point trials was lowest for high H (57.1 ± 4.1%) then improved steadily for intermediate (71.4 ± 1.2%) and low H (81.1 ± 2.2%).
source: In contrast, accuracy on non change-point trials with the same strength of evidence was lowest for high H (57.1 ± 4.1%) then improved steadily for intermediate (71.4 ± 1.2%) and low H (81.1 ± 2.2%; Spearman's correlation between non change-point accuracy and H was −0.502, p < 0.0001, vs a normative prediction of −0.625; Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence and reference to Figure 5G,H.

claim: In the triangles task with strong evidence, the trade-off between change detection and steady signal identification was much smaller than with weak evidence.
source: When the evidence was strong, the trade-off was much smaller, as predicted by the normative model (Spearman's correlation between change-point accuracy and H was −0.040, p = 0.557 and between non change-point accuracy and H was −0.005, p = 0.945; normative predictions were 0.027 and 0.010, respectively; Figure 5J,K).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence and reference to Figure 5J,K.

claim: Direct estimates of the mapping of subjective beliefs to priors from triangles task choice data depended on subjective H.
source: Third, we used choice data to directly estimate the mapping of subjective beliefs to priors (Ln − 1 to Ψn, Figure 6; compare to Figure 1B). Like for the normative model, the estimated mappings depended on subjective H (one-way MANOVA for the groups shown in Figure 6A, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence and reference to Figure 6 and Figure 1B.

claim: For each H-group in the triangles task, the estimated mappings of subjective beliefs to priors matched predictions of the normative model.
source: Moreover, for each H-group, these mappings matched predictions of the normative model (Figure 6B,E; Hotelling's t-test comparing data and model, p = 0.189, 0.321, and 0.086 for low, medium, and high values of objective H, respectively).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence and reference to Figure 6B,E.

claim: The leaky-accumulator model had worse overall fits to the triangles task choice data than the normative model for 34 of 48 subjects.
source: The leaky-accumulator model had worse overall fits to the choice data than the normative model for 34 of 48 subjects (median ± SEM difference in BIC = −5.179 ± 1.967, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.0001)
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: The leaky-accumulator model predicted mappings of subjective beliefs to priors that matched the triangles task pooled data only for medium and high values of H but not for low values of H.
source: and predicted mappings of subjective beliefs to priors that matched the pooled data only for medium and high values of H but not for low values of H, which lacked the asymptotic regime prescribed by the normative model when beliefs were more certain (Figure 6C,F; Hotelling's t-test, p < 0.0001 for low objective H, and p = 0.312 and 0.545 for medium and high objective H, respectively).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence and reference to Figure 6C,F.

claim: The model with perfect accumulation to a hazard-specific stabilizing boundary had worse overall fits to the triangles task choice data than the normative model for 34 of 48 subjects.
source: Likewise, the model with perfect accumulation to a hazard-specific stabilizing boundary had worse overall fits to the choice data than the normative model for 34 of 48 subjects (−0.942 ± 0.487, p = 0.007)
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: The bounded-accumulator model lacked the leaky-accumulation regime prescribed by the normative model when beliefs were uncertain and H was high.
source: reflecting the lack of a leaky-accumulation regime prescribed by the normative model when beliefs were uncertain and H was high (Figure 6D,G; Hotelling's t-test, p = 0.228, 0.463, and 0.017, respectively).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence and reference to Figure 6D,G.

claim: The dots-reversal task was a novel version of a commonly used random-dot motion task.
source: This task was a novel version of a commonly used random-dot motion task (Britten et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: In the dots-reversal task, the direction of coherent motion underwent sudden changes within trials.
source: For this 'dots-reversal' task, the direction of coherent motion underwent sudden changes within trials.
evidence: This is stated in the task description.

claim: Each subject in the dots-reversal task participated in two separate sessions, one in which changes occurred at a relatively slow rate (0.1 Hz), and one in which changes occurred at a fast rate (2.0 Hz).
source: Each subject participated in two separate sessions, one in which changes occurred at a relatively slow rate (0.1 Hz), and one in which changes occurred at a fast rate (2.0 Hz) rate (Figure 7, Videos 1–4).
evidence: This is stated in the task description with reference to Figure 7 and Videos 1–4.

claim: In the dots-reversal task, motion strength (coherence) was fixed to either a high or low value within each trial.
source: Motion strength (coherence) was fixed to either a high or low value within each trial, and subjects were instructed to pay attention to the stimulus throughout the trial and then indicate its final direction, after which they received feedback on the correct answer.
evidence: This is stated in the task description.

claim: Models that allowed subjective λ to vary with objective λ provided better fits to the dots-reversal task data than a model that ignored the session-specific changes in λ.
source: Models that allowed subjective λ (change-point rate, here treated as a continuous-time variable) to vary with objective λ provided better fits to the data than a model that ignored the session-specific changes in λ (median ± SEM difference in BIC from the normative vs block-independent model fits was −4.790 ± 1.216, p < 0.0005; per subject, normative BIC values were significantly lower in 9 of 13 subjects with a Bonferroni corrected p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: The normative model performed well on the dots-reversal task, with choice residuals centered around zero (mean ± std deviance residual = 0.053 ± 0.897).
source: The normative model performed well overall, with choice residuals centered around zero (mean ± std deviance residual = 0.053 ± 0.897) and a reasonably close match to the choice data (median ± bootstrapped SEM McFadden r2 of 0.385 ± 0.055 across subjects).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: In the dots-reversal task, 12 of 13 subjects had best-fitting values of adaptive, subjective λ that showed appropriate sensitivity to objective λ.
source: Of the 13 subjects, 12 had best-fitting values of adaptive, subjective λ that showed appropriate sensitivity to objective λ, with estimated subjective λ lower on 0.1 vs 2.0 Hz trials (Figure 7B; Wilcoxon signed-rank p < 0.05).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence and reference to Figure 7B.

claim: In the dots-reversal task, subjects tended to overestimate low values and underestimate high values of λ.
source: However, like for the triangles task, the subjects tended to overestimate low values and underestimate high values of λ (median ± bootstrapped SEM estimated subjective λ = 0.365 ± 0.109 and 1.129 ± 0.168 Hz for the 0.1-Hz and 2-Hz conditions respectively)
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: For high-coherence trials in the dots-reversal task, the strong sensory evidence dominated the decision process, yielding >90% accuracy within 500 ms following the final change in direction irrespective of the rate of preceding direction changes.
source: For high-coherence trials, the strong sensory evidence dominated the decision process, yielding >90% accuracy within 500 ms following the final change in direction irrespective of the rate of preceding direction changes (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 8D,E.

claim: For low-coherence trials in the dots-reversal task, integration times were strongly dependent on hazard rate.
source: In contrast, for low-coherence trials, integration times were strongly dependent on hazard rate (i.e., greater effects of ψ in Equation 1)
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: For low-coherence trials in the dots-reversal task, performance was worse for the 0.1-Hz condition for durations <500 ms, reflecting persistence of the perceived direction of motion just prior to the final change-point.
source: Specifically, accuracy improved more steeply as a function of viewing duration for the low- vs high-hazard condition: performance was worse for the 0.1-Hz condition for durations <500 ms, reflecting persistence of the perceived direction of motion just prior to the final change-point (i.e., direction reversal), but rose as viewing duration increased and exceeded performance for the 2-Hz condition at long durations (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 8A,B.

claim: For low-coherence trials in the dots-reversal task, choice accuracy was lower for the low-hazard condition just following a change-point (7.1 ± 11.1% and 40.3 ± 2.8%, for low- and high-hazard sessions respectively, when the stimulus was shown for <300 ms following the final change-point).
source: For low-coherence trials, choice accuracy was lower for the low-hazard condition just following a change-point (median ± bootstrapped SEM 7.1 ± 11.1% and 40.3 ± 2.8%, for low- and high-hazard sessions respectively, when the stimulus was shown for <300 ms following the final change-point, Wilcoxon signed rank, p < 0.01, vs predicted accuracies of 34.6 ± 4.7% and 44.9 ± 3.1%, respectively)
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: For low-coherence trials in the dots-reversal task, choice accuracy was greater for the low-hazard condition for viewing durations >300 ms following the final change-point (83.6 ± 3.6% and 69.9 ± 8.3%, respectively).
source: but was greater for the low-hazard condition thereafter (83.6 ± 3.6% and 69.9 ± 8.3%, respectively, p < 0.0005, vs predicted 86.2 ± 2.3% and 74.2 ± 2.9%, respectively).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: For high-coherence trials in the dots-reversal task, choice accuracy showed a weaker trade-off, with no difference by hazard-rate condition for short viewing durations following the final change point.
source: For high-coherence trials, choice accuracy was much higher overall and, consistent with the normative model, showed a weaker trade-off, with no difference by hazard-rate condition for short viewing durations following the final change point (66.7 ± 14.6% and 66.1 ± 7.3% for 0.1-Hz and 2-Hz sessions respectively, p = 0.831, vs predicted 46.9 ± 9.4% and 59.7 ± 3.7%, respectively)
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: In the dots-reversal task, the best-fitting leak depended on both hazard rate and motion coherence level.
source: Third, we directly measured the dependence of choice dynamics on both the hazard rate and the strength of the sensory evidence by fitting choice data to integrating models with separate leaks for each hazard-specific session and coherence level (Figure 9). As predicted by the normative model (Figures 3A, 8B,E), the best-fitting leak depended on both (Friedman test, p < 0.0005 for the effect of hazard rate and p < 0.0001 for the effect of motion coherence; Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence and reference to Figure 9 and other figures.

claim: The per-subject, pairwise differences between best-fitting leak in the dots-reversal task, computed with respect to either coherence or hazard rate, did not differ from predictions of the normative model.
source: The per-subject, pairwise differences between best-fitting leak, computed with respect to either coherence or hazard rate, did not differ from predictions of the normative model (median ± bootstrapped SEM normalized data–model difference by hazard rate = −0.003 ± 0.021, by coherence = −0.001 ± 0.050, Wilcoxon signed rank p = 0.501 and 0.292, respectively).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: The leaky-integrator model, in which the leak depended on hazard rate but not coherence level, had worse overall fits to the dots-reversal task choice data than the normative model for 10 of 13 subjects.
source: The leaky-integrator model, in which the leak depended on hazard rate but not coherence level, had worse overall fits to the choice data than the normative model for 10 of 13 subjects (median ± bootstrapped SEM difference in BIC = −4.066 ± 3.078, Wilcoxon signed rank, p < 0.05)
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: The normative model outperformed the model with perfect integration to a stabilizing boundary that freely varied by objective hazard rate in the dots-reversal task (BIC was lower for 9 of 13 subjects).
source: The normative model also outperformed the model with perfect integration to a stabilizing boundary that freely varied by objective hazard rate (BIC was lower for 9 of 13 subjects, −4.305 ± 2.662, p < 0.05).
evidence: This is stated with statistical evidence.

claim: The normative model of evidence accumulation is based on Bayesian principles for inferring changes in the statistics of a generative process.
source: We derived a normative model of evidence accumulation for decision tasks that is based on Bayesian principles for inferring changes in the statistics of a generative process (Rabiner, 1989; Adams and MacKay, 2007; Behrens et al., 2007; Fearnhead and Liu, 2007; Brown and Steyvers, 2009; Wilson and Finkel, 2009; Nassar et al., 2010, 2012; Wilson et al., 2010; Boerlin et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2013; Gonzalez Castro et al., 2014; McGuire et al., 2014; Sato and Kording, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: The normative model incorporates change detection into sequential-sampling decision models.
source: Our model incorporates change detection into sequential-sampling decision models and is related to other, modified versions of these models that have been used to combine multiple sensory cues of different but known reliabilities or infer unknown sensory reliability assumed to be stable during the course of decision-making (Hanks et al., 2011; Deneve, 2012; Drugowitsch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: The normative model casts adaptation directly in the context of the evidence-accumulation process.
source: However, unlike those models, which invoked a separate learning-rate term or had other, more complex forms, our model casts adaptation directly in the context of the evidence-accumulation process that is a key focus of studies of decision-making (Usher and McClelland, 2001; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Huk and Shadlen, 2005; Uchida et al., 2006; Brunton et al., 2013; Hanks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to contrast with other models.

claim: Human subjects made decisions on two separate tasks that were consistent with the adaptive, hazard-dependent accumulation process prescribed by the model.
source: We showed that human subjects made decisions on two separate tasks, requiring evidence accumulation either across or within trials, that were consistent with the adaptive, hazard-dependent accumulation process prescribed by the model.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding.

claim: Subjects could both learn a range of hazard rates and then use those learned rates in a normative manner to interpret sequences of evidence to make decisions.
source: Specifically, we showed that subjects could both learn a range of hazard rates and then use those learned rates in a normative manner to interpret sequences of evidence to make decisions.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding.

claim: Subjects tended to learn hazard rates imperfectly, over-estimating low hazard rates and under-estimating high hazard rates.
source: However, they tended to learn imperfectly, over-estimating low hazard rates and under-estimating high hazard rates.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding.

claim: Deviations from optimality in subjects' decisions can be interpreted as different, hazard-dependent set-points of an inherent trade-off between sensitivity to change and sensitivity to steady-state signals.
source: Our framework provides a new way to interpret these deviations from optimality: not simply as poor performance, but rather as different, hazard-dependent set-points of an inherent trade-off. This tradeoff balances sensitivity to change during periods of expected instability, and sensitivity to steady-state signals during periods of expected stability.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Prior expectations about a lack of perfect environmental stability might provide new insights into previous studies of the temporal dynamics of evidence accumulation.
source: Such prior expectations about a lack of perfect environmental stability interpreted in the context of our framework might also provide new insights into previous studies of the temporal dynamics of evidence accumulation.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about implications.

claim: Deviations from perfect accumulation in the brain might reflect normative adjustments to expected instabilities, even under nominally stable conditions.
source: In contrast, our results imply that at least some deviations from perfect accumulation might reflect normative adjustments to expected instabilities, even under the nominally stable conditions used for many tasks.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the findings.

claim: Leaky accumulation that places more emphasis on recent vs past information might reflect prior expectations that instabilities are likely to occur within a given time frame.
source: For example, leaky accumulation that places more emphasis on recent vs past information or rates of accumulation that vary as a function of time, which can account for the temporal dynamics of certain decisions about stimuli that are presented with stable statistics for 100's of ms or more, might reflect prior expectations that instabilities are likely to occur within that time frame (Usher and McClelland, 2001; Eckhoff et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with citations.

claim: Reports of an 'urgency' signal that limits temporal integration might reflect expectations of impending instabilities.
source: Likewise, reports of an 'urgency' signal that limits temporal integration based on a drive to respond quickly might reflect similar expectations of impending instabilities (Reddi and Carpenter, 2000; Ditterich, 2006; Cisek et al., 2009; Drugowitsch et al., 2012; Thura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with citations.

claim: The temporal integration window for many kinds of decisions might be highly flexible and adapt to the temporal dynamics of the environment.
source: These interpretations are consistent with the idea that the temporal integration window for many kinds of decisions might be highly flexible and adapt to the temporal dynamics of the environment (Ossmy et al., 2013; Gonzalez Castro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: The accumulated evidence that serves as the decision variable governing choice behavior can also be thought of as a confidence signal.
source: Insofar as the accumulated evidence that serves as the decision variable governing choice behavior can also be thought of as a confidence signal, such adaptive dynamics might also pertain to confidence judgments associated with certain decision tasks (Kepecs et al., 2008; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Ma and Jazayeri, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: In the normative model, the adaptive accumulation process can be suspended by the non-linear dynamics of the accumulation process itself, not by an extrinsically imposed decision rule like an absorbing decision boundary.
source: Alternatively, in our model the adaptive accumulation process can be suspended, at least temporarily, not by an extrinsically imposed decision rule like an absorbing decision boundary but rather by the non-linear dynamics of the accumulation process itself.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the model.

claim: 48 subjects (29 female, 19 male; age range = 19–45 years) participated in the triangles task.
source: 48 subjects (29 female, 19 male; age range = 19–45 years) participated in the triangles task
evidence: This is stated in the methods.

source: and 13 subjects (7 female, 6 male; age range = 19–38 years) participated in the dots-reversal task after providing informed consent.
evidence: This is stated in the methods.

source: Human subject protocols were approved by the University of Pennsylvania Internal Review Board.
